> ## MAYBE — полезно, но не первое окно
>
> **Lürzer’s Archive** — сильный curated advertising archive: заявляет 40 лет и 42K+ ads/TV/digital work, плюс current “Best ads” features. ([Lurzers Archive][10]) Я бы держал как secondary source, потому что он силён как профессиональный архив, но для этого конкретного запроса быстрое подтверждение “object+integrated typography inside one frame” слабее, чем у The Work / AdForum / Ads of the World.
>
> **One Club / ADC Awards Archive** — хороший award archive с фильтрами по Advertising, Photography, Packaging Design, Typography/Lettering, Products/Commercial и категориями Beauty/Cosmetics, Beverage, Food, Posters, Print. ([oneclub.org][11]) Но как hunting surface он менее прямой: больше awards database, чем визуальная reference-поверхность. Использовать, когда нужен craft validation.
>
> **The Brand Identity** — часто очень хороший для modern brand/product systems; свежие результаты показывают Nothing Ear (3) campaign with earbuds, dot-matrix typography and still-life direction, а также product photography/typography cases. ([The Brand Identity][12]) Но сайт хуже отдался при проверке, поэтому я не ставлю его в KEEP без стабильной верификации.
>
> **Packaging of the World** — searchable и свежий, но шумный/self-submitted. Полезен для long-tail packaging-led finds, например Nourvie 2026, где photography described as extension of packaging design, or 2025 skincare/product photography cases. ([packagingoftheworld.com][13]) Не ставлю выше из-за uneven quality и большого количества mockup-like материала.
>

> ## AVOID / down-rank for this task
>
> **Pinterest** — даёт visual scatter, но слабую provenance, плохую повторяемость и много “ideas boards”; даже релевантные board results вроде “Advertising, Product & Still Life Photography” остаются просто pin collections. ([Pinterest][14])
>
> **Behance broad search** — можно найти gems, но сигнал очень грязный: результаты по shoe/beauty campaign заполнены low-view social media ads, mockups, student/spec work и generic portfolio uploads. ([Behance][15])
>
> **Awwwards / Webflow-style galleries** — down-rank: это web/UI awards, не product-object advertising archive. Awwwards прямо позиционируется как website awards / web design trends surface. ([Awwwards][16])
>
> **Generic “poster inspiration” / trend blogs / stock libraries** — слишком много абстрактных постеров, templates, AI prompts, “text over image” и decorative typography без реального commercial product frame.
>
> ---
>
> ## Где искать первым
>
> Для **modern product/object + integrated typography in advertising** я бы шёл так:
>
> 1. **The Work / Cannes Lions** — если нужен топовый commercial craft и recent award-level references.
> 2. **AdForum + Ads of the World** — если нужно быстро собрать много реальных product campaigns и руками отсеять.
> 3. **GoSee.NEWS / STILLSTARS** — если главный критерий: photographed object, still-life, lighting, crop, silhouette.
> 4. **BP&O + The Dieline** — если нужен packaging-led product world, где typography и object/packaging неразделимы.
> 5. **Fonts In Use** — когда нужно докопаться именно до typographic logic, а не просто mood.

Я понял так: проблема не в паре неудачных ссылок, а в самом **паттерне ошибки**. Мы пропустили в shortlist три типа мусора:

- `не туда по объекту` — UI/UX экраны вместо малых текстовых приемов; fashion/editorial/campaign surfaces без предметки;
- `формально релевантно, но practically useless` — платно, тяжело искать, слабая навигация, poor repeatability;
- `архивно/институционально ок, но stylistically dead или не твой класс сигнала`.

И да, самый явный провал сейчас:
- по `фото + текст` сигнал очень слабый;
- по `мелким текстовым модулям` мы уехали в `screen libraries`, хотя тебе нужны отдельные графические/типографические приемы, почти как постерные детали, а не app flows.

Туман сейчас в одном месте: нам важно не просто удалить это из HTML, а **понять статус исключения**.

1. Эти источники надо считать `глобально запрещенными` для всех будущих поисков в этом проекте, или часть из них банится только в конкретных ветках?
   Например: `Mobbin/Refero/Page Flows` — бан только для text modules, или вообще больше никогда не предлагать.

2. Ты хочешь, чтобы я их:
   - просто убрал из дашборда,
   - или убрал **и** добавил отдельный `Rejected / Do Not Suggest` registry с причиной отказа?

3. Для ветки `мелкие текстовые приемы` правильно ли я формулирую новый критерий так:
   нужны не экраны и не UI patterns, а **отдельные композиционные текстовые элементы** —
   `ступеньки`, `плашки`, `рамки`, `наклейки`, `диагональные наборы`, `caption/callout fragments`, `poster-like text devices`, `annotation systems`, `micro typographic constructions`?

- вычищу дашборд,
- зафиксирую blacklist,
- и перепишу правила так, чтобы это больше не всплывало как “подходящий ресурс”.

А у тебя дыра в другом месте: **реальные deployed commercial assets среднего сегмента**, где `товар + текст` живут не как “дизайн-объект”, а как рабочий продающий носитель.

То есть проблема, кажется, не в том, что таких кейсов нет. Проблема в том, что мы искали **не тот класс поверхностей**. Pinterest их иногда показывает как обрывки, но мы не дошли до их исходных носителей.

Туман сейчас в одном месте:
нам надо определить не “стиль”, а **carrier layer**. Где именно этот объект живет:
- `stories / paid social statics`
- `баннеры / promo tiles / sale cards`
- `marketplace/storefront creatives`
- `email hero / ecommerce promo modules`
- `retail / in-store / OOH lite`

Вот 3 вопроса, которые реально меняют поиск:

1. Что для тебя сейчас главный носитель, который хочется пробить первым: `stories`, `баннеры`, `e-commerce promo`, `marketplace creatives` или `retail posters`?

2. Ты готова брать **средний сегмент даже если он визуально местами грубее**, но там есть полезная механика `товар+текст`?
   Или нам нужен только `middle-market but still visually above sludge`?

Что я бы считал реальными оставшимися дырами:
- нет eval-набора: это теперь главный пробел;
- нет отдельного `bad-vocabulary` файла, но он пока не обязателен;
- история нам пока правда не нужна шире, чем white/black lists.

Про `BadTags / BadVocab`: нет, это не надо вести “методом тыка”.
Правильнее так:
- добавлять только после повторяющегося сбоя;
- фиксировать не просто слово, а `слово -> какой drift вызывает -> в какой ветке запрещено -> чем заменять`;
- держать это branch-specific, а не “на все случаи жизни”;
- не раздувать список заранее.

То есть правило простое: если термин дважды уводит не туда, или один раз уводит совсем в другой класс объектов, его уже можно заносить.

По твоему вопросу про ChatGPT и “второй чат подтягивает результат первого”: да, это может происходить не только у тебя в голове. По официальной справке OpenAI:
- если ты работаешь **внутри одного Project**, чаты могут ссылаться на другие чаты в этом же проекте; в некоторых режимах память проекта вообще специально держит контекст внутри проекта: [Projects in ChatGPT](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10169521-using-projects-in-chatgpt%23.ejs)
- если у тебя включены **Memory / Reference chat history**, ChatGPT может использовать прошлые чаты и сохраненные воспоминания между разговорами: [What is Memory?](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8983136-what-) и [Memory FAQ](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8590148-memory-faq%3Dhelp.openai.com%26lng%3Den)
- если нужен реально чистый прогон, надо использовать **Temporary Chat**: он не использует память и не ссылается на прошлые разговоры, хотя кастомные инструкции все равно остаются: [Temporary Chat FAQ](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8914046-temporary-chat-faq)

То есть если результаты “подозрительно похожи”, самые вероятные причины:
- ты в одном Project;
- включена memory/chat history;
- промпты по форме слишком похожи и модель падает в один и тот же safe pattern.

Практически что делать:
1. Для независимой проверки запускать новый prompt в `Temporary Chat`.
2. Если работаешь в Projects, учитывать, что соседние чаты могут влиять.
3. Для red-team сравнений лучше делать либо `Temporary Chat`, либо отдельный Project.

**Final prompt**
```text
Проведи manual web search mapping pass и выясни, где вообще живут и публикуются реальные commercial compositions, в которых текст и фото работают как один кадр.

Ищу не “красивые постеры вообще” и не один конкретный носитель. Носитель вторичен. Это могут быть stories, paid social statics, banners, promo tiles, OOH, covers, retail promo visuals, email hero-like assets, agency cases, production studio work и другие carrier layers. Главный критерий один: текст и фото должны быть композиционно связаны внутри одного visual, желательно вокруг предмета / товара / product object.

Цель этого прохода:
не shortlist, а map the field.
Нужно понять, какие вообще существуют source ecosystems, carrier layers и publication patterns для такого материала, чтобы потом уже делать отдельный shortlist.

Важно:
- не уходи в luxury-safe layer как в единственную зону;
- ищи mixed field: luxury + middle-market + mass-commercial;
- допускай более грубый middle/mass layer, но фильтруй low-grade sludge;
- marketplace исключить;
- не уводи поиск в web/UI galleries, UX screen libraries, movie-poster/cinema archives, museum/institutional poster collections, fashion campaign indexes без явного product+type proof;
- не подменяй задачу “text over image” примерами, где это просто подпись поверх фото.

Что считать валидным source:
- surface, где такие кейсы реально публикуются;
- или post-factum reference surface, где их можно регулярно добывать;
- case structure считается полезным;
- credits, archive logic, repeatability, wayfinding to similar work — сильные плюсы, но не все обязательны одновременно.

Что нужно вернуть:
1. Map of the field:
   - какие carrier layers вообще существуют для product/object + integrated text;
   - где такие работы публикуются вживую;
   - где они собираются после факта как references;
   - какие source classes для этого поля реально рабочие.
2. Source ecosystems:
   - agency case-study surfaces;
   - production / still-life / commercial photography surfaces;
   - brand campaign / promo publication surfaces;
   - editorial / publishing-adjacent surfaces, если они реально пересекаются с нужным объектом;
   - any other valid publication ecosystems that repeatedly produce this material.
3. For each source class:
   - почему он релевантен;
   - какой carrier layer он покрывает;
   - насколько там реально искать middle/mass-commercial, а не только luxury;
   - где signal сильный, а где начинается мусор.
4. Explicit gaps:
   - какие зоны поля почти не индексируются напрямую;
   - где Pinterest, вероятно, показывает derivative fragments, но не source-of-origin.
5. End with:
   - recommended next-pass research plan for building a shortlist.

Anti-surface requirements:
- Do not treat top-ranked or easily found results as strong by default.
- Run at least one source-constrained pass, one contradiction-seeking pass, and one deeper expansion pass.
- Prefer fewer stronger source ecosystems over padded completeness.
- If a visible result is kept, explain why it survived over less visible alternatives.
```

**Prompt notes**
- mode: manual web search
- freshness window: prioritize 2024–2026
- source bias: source ecosystems, carrier layers, case structures, live publication surfaces
- scope cut: map first, no shortlist yet

**Final prompt**
```text
Task:
Run a manual web-search mapping pass to find where real commercial compositions live in which text and photo function as one composed frame.

Object:
I am not looking for “beautiful posters” or one specific carrier. The carrier is secondary. This can include stories, paid social statics, promo banners, retail promo visuals, OOH-lite, covers, brand campaign assets, agency case-study visuals, production studio work, and adjacent commercial formats. The primary rule is: text and photo must be compositionally tied inside one visual, ideally around a product / object / item, not just headline over image.

Goal:
Map the field first, not shortlist it yet. I need to understand which source ecosystems, carrier layers, publication patterns, and case structures actually produce and publish this material so that a later shortlist can be built on the right layer.

Primary rule:
Do not default to luxury-safe surfaces. Map a mixed field: luxury + middle-market + mass-commercial, while filtering out low-grade sludge.

Exclude:
- marketplace creatives and marketplace surfaces;
- UI/UX screen libraries, app-flow databases, and web galleries;
- movie-poster / cinema archives;
- museum / institutional poster archives;
- fashion campaign indexes unless they show explicit product/object + integrated type proof;
- generic ad directories that create clutter without repeatable hunting value;
- banal “text over image” where text does not materially interact with the photo.

Source logic:
- prefer agency case-study surfaces, production/still-life/commercial photography surfaces, brand campaign publication surfaces, credited commercial work, and reference surfaces with case structure or repeatable browsing paths;
- include live publication surfaces and post-factum reference surfaces if they reliably expose this object class;
- treat credits, archive logic, repeatability, and wayfinding to similar work as strong positives, but not all are mandatory at once.

Freshness logic:
Prioritize current evidence from 2024–2026, especially 2025–2026. If a source class is older, keep it only if it still has clear operational value for finding contemporary product/object + text work.

What to return:
1. A field map of the main source ecosystems and carrier layers where this material actually appears.
2. For each source class: why it is relevant, what carrier layers it covers, whether it tends toward luxury / middle / mass, and where signal turns into noise.
3. A split between:
   - where this work is published live,
   - where it is collected after the fact as reference.
4. Explicit blind spots: which zones are poorly indexed and where Pinterest likely shows derivative fragments rather than the original publishing surface.
5. End with a recommended next-pass plan for building a shortlist.

Anti-surface requirements:
- Do not treat top-ranked or easily found results as strong by default.
- Run at least one source-constrained pass, one contradiction-seeking pass, and one deeper expansion pass.
- Prefer fewer stronger source ecosystems over padded completeness.
- If an obvious visible result survives, explain why it beat deeper alternatives.
```

- Freshness window: `2024–2026`, strongest bias to `2025–2026`

> (Below is a **field map**, not a shortlist. I’m treating the target object as: **commercial frames where product/object photography and type are co-designed into one visual system**, not merely a caption/headline placed over an image.
>
> ## What survived the mapping pass
>
> The strongest source layer is a **four-part ecosystem**:
>
> 1. **Agency / brand case-study pages**
> 2. **Award archives and curated advertising databases**
> 3. **Production, still-life, photography, and post-production surfaces**
> 4. **Trade/editorial campaign publications**
>
> A fifth layer—**live paid-social/ad transparency libraries**—is useful for current evidence, but weak for craft attribution and wayfinding.
>
> ---
>
> # 1. Main source ecosystems and carrier layers
>
> ## A. Agency and brand-owned case-study surfaces
>
> **Why relevant:**
> This is the cleanest layer when the work is a real commercial campaign, because it often preserves the strategic idea, creative credits, roll-out logic, and media/carrier scope. It is especially useful when type is not decoration but the campaign mechanism: price labels, packaging typography, product naming systems, object-shaped type, or product-as-message.
>
> Good evidence from this pass: **PENNY “Price Packs”** by Serviceplan, where price becomes packaging design and OOH; **Cadbury “Made to Share”**, where the pack itself is the typographic/compositional device; and IKEA campaigns where product, copy, price tag, and image are inseparable rather than layered. ([house-of-communication.com][1])
>
> **Carrier layers covered:**
> Packaging-as-ad, OOH, print, retail POS, campaign statics, social campaign assets, launch films, case films, sometimes in-store or e-commerce extensions.
>
> **Market bias:**
> Mixed. This layer is strong for **middle-market and mass-commercial** because supermarkets, FMCG, furniture, wellness, food, beauty, and retail brands often use object-plus-type systems. It also covers luxury, but luxury is not dominant unless the agency’s client roster skews that way.
>
> **Where signal turns into noise:**
> The case film can exaggerate the “system” while hiding the actual static assets. Also, many agency pages prioritize idea/results over downloadable visual variants. Good next-pass behavior: use agency case pages as **truth anchors**, then chase the actual stills through trade press, award archives, and production credits.
>
> ---
>
> ## B. Award archives and curated advertising databases
>
> **Why relevant:**
> Award archives are good for work where **type, image, product, and carrier are judged as craft**, especially in Print & Outdoor, Typography/Lettering, Packaging, Design, and Product Design categories. ADC/The One Club, D&AD, ADCE, Epica, AdForum, Lürzer’s Archive, and Ads of the World all surfaced relevant paths. ADC explicitly separates disciplines such as Packaging Design, Photography, Product Design, and Typography/Lettering; ADCE’s Annual of Annuals lets you browse by year, work, creatives, agencies, categories, and countries. ([ADC Awards][2])
>
> **Carrier layers covered:**
> Print, OOH, packaging, brand systems, campaign case boards, retail activation, occasionally social/static campaign extensions.
>
> **Market bias:**
> Mixed but skewed toward **awardable concepts**. This helps avoid sludge, but creates another bias: clever, juror-friendly ideas over everyday commercial volume. Mass-market work can appear when the idea is simple and strong—PENNY, IKEA, Cadbury—but routine retail promo work is underrepresented.
>
> **Where signal turns into noise:**
> Generic ad databases can become clutter fast. Ads of the World has repeatable filters for campaigns, media, industry, country, and agency, but its results include student/spec work, thin uploads, generic packaging redesigns, and banal text-over-product layouts. It is useful as a **broad trawler**, not as a final authority. AdForum is stronger when tied to award entries or agency pages, but less good as a blind search surface. ([Ads of the World™][3])
>
> **Why obvious visible results survived:**
> IKEA, Cadbury, and PENNY survive not because they are easy to find, but because the **commercial mechanism is the composition**: price tag as story, pack as social division, price as pack identity. These are not “nice posters”; they are product/object/type systems with repeatable carrier logic. ([Creative Review][4])
>
> ---
>
> ## C. Production, still-life, commercial photography, and post-production surfaces
>
> **Why relevant:**
> This is the best ecosystem for finding **object-led commercial imagery before it becomes a public campaign page**. Production Paradise’s 2025 still-life issues are especially useful because they group commercial photographers and studios by still-life/product work, spanning beauty, food, drink, fashion, skincare, tech, everyday goods, and luxury. One 2025 issue explicitly frames the set as “Luxury & everyday brands” from PG Tips to Hermès; another includes product imagery from Hilton, Laneige, Kronenbourg, Cadbury, and more. ([Production Paradise][5])
>
> **Carrier layers covered:**
> Still-life campaign photography, product hero imagery, retail/social assets, trade-show displays, storefront billboards, beauty/fashion/food/drink product systems, motion loops, CGI/post-production composites.
>
> **Market bias:**
> Very mixed. This layer is unusually good for avoiding luxury-only bias because commercial photographers shoot both everyday and premium products. It also exposes the **middle layer**—food/drink, beauty, wellness, tech accessories, homeware—that design press often misses.
>
> **Where signal turns into noise:**
> The main weakness is that many photographer/production portfolios show the **image before final typography**. You may find brilliant object photography but not the completed text-photo frame. The right method is to use these pages to identify photographers, production companies, retouchers, and clients, then cross-search the campaign name or brand in agency/trade/award sources.
>
> ---
>
> ## D. Trade and editorial campaign publications
>
> **Why relevant:**
> Creative Review, It’s Nice That, LBB, Campaign, The Drum, Creative Boom, Famous Campaigns, Design Week, and similar publications are useful because they publish recent commercial work with **credits, carrier notes, strategic framing, and enough editorial curation to reduce sludge**.
>
> Examples from this pass: Creative Review covered IKEA’s 2025 Swedish campaign where price tags become central storytelling elements, including agency and production credits; LBB and Campaign covered Holland & Barrett’s 2026 “Back Your Body” OOH/design system, where photographed body parts form type; The Drum and Creative Salon covered Cadbury’s “Made to Share” campaign and its commercial results/return. ([Creative Review][4])
>
> **Carrier layers covered:**
> OOH, print, social statics, campaign launches, brand platforms, packaging campaigns, retail activations, sometimes in-house brand work.
>
> **Market bias:**
> Middle-to-premium commercial. Creative Review and It’s Nice That skew design/craft; Campaign and The Drum skew advertising/business; Famous Campaigns skews PR/earned-media hooks; LBB is useful for production and credits. Together they provide a healthier mix than any one of them alone.
>
> **Where signal turns into noise:**
> Trade publications often over-index on novelty and launch news. They also publish a lot of film-led work where the stills are secondary. The signal is strongest when the article includes **static visuals, campaign credits, media/carrier description, and a named agency/production company**.
>
> ---
>
> ## E. Packaging / identity / design-publication surfaces
>
> **Why relevant:**
> Packaging and identity publications are strong when the text is physically bound to the object: labels, wrappers, cartons, sleeves, hangtags, price labels, and product systems. This is a neighboring but important zone because many commercial frames are not “ads” first; they are **packaging systems photographed as campaign assets**.
>
> Dieline is a useful broad source for packaging innovation and brand design, with a constant flow of consumer goods, home/garden, food/drink, and beauty packaging. But it can drift toward identity-system documentation rather than real campaign-frame proof. ([DIELINE][6])
>
> **Carrier layers covered:**
> Packaging, retail promo visuals, product launch imagery, brand-world stills, shelf/promo systems, case-study mockups.
>
> **Market bias:**
> Strong for FMCG, food/drink, beauty, wellness, home goods, DTC, and premium consumer goods. Less useful for service brands unless the identity includes physical artifacts.
>
> **Where signal turns into noise:**
> Mockups. Beautiful packaging renders are not always commercial compositions in circulation. The next pass should distinguish **live packaging photographed or advertised** from studio mockups made for a design case study.
>
> ---
>
> ## F. Live paid-social and ad transparency libraries
>
> **Why relevant:**
> This is the layer closest to live commercial use. Meta’s Ad Library lets users search currently running ads across Meta technologies by keyword or advertiser; Google’s Ads Transparency Center is a searchable hub for ads from verified advertisers; TikTok Creative Center exposes top-performing ads, trends, and creative examples. ([Facebook][7])
>
> **Carrier layers covered:**
> Paid social statics, short-form video covers, carousel frames, performance creative, product promo variants, offer-led retail creative.
>
> **Market bias:**
> Mass and middle-market. This is where many real product/type/photo statics live, especially beauty, food, retail, wellness, apparel, and home goods.
>
> **Where signal turns into noise:**
> Very high noise. Most paid-social work is banal text overlay, templated offer creative, or marketplace-style product tiles. These libraries are useful only after you have **brand targets, category targets, or known campaign names**. They are poor for open-ended aesthetic discovery.
>
> ---
>
> # 2. Live publication vs post-factum reference
>
> ## Published live / near-live
>
> These are where the work appears closest to its commercial deployment:
>
> | Live layer                                       | Usefulness                                     | Weakness                                             |
> | ------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
> | Brand social channels and campaign landing pages | Best for actual deployed frames and variants   | Poor indexing, assets disappear, no credits          |
> | Meta / Google / TikTok ad libraries              | Best for current paid-social evidence          | High sludge; limited craft/context; weak attribution |
> | Retail / brand email / in-store / POS captures   | Strong for mass-commercial product-type frames | Poorly indexed, often private or ephemeral           |
> | OOH reporting and trade-launch articles          | Good for carrier proof and campaign timing     | Often only 1–3 hero images                           |
> | Agency launch posts                              | Good for credits and rationale                 | Often selective, case-film biased                    |
>
> ## Collected after the fact
>
> These are better for building a shortlist because they preserve context and wayfinding:
>
> | Reference layer                                        | Usefulness                                          | Weakness                          |
> | ------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
> | Agency case studies                                    | Strongest strategic and credit anchor               | Selective, polished               |
> | Award archives: D&AD, ADC, ADCE, One Show, Epica       | Strong filters by discipline, year, medium, country | Award-bait bias                   |
> | AdForum / Lürzer’s / Ads of the World                  | Repeatable browsing and database behavior           | Varying quality; generic clutter  |
> | Production Paradise / photographer reps / post studios | Best object-photography trail                       | Often lacks final integrated type |
> | Trade publications                                     | Strong recent campaign discovery                    | Editorial novelty bias            |
> | Packaging/design publications                          | Strong for object-bound type systems                | Mockup/design-case drift          |
>
> ---
>
> # 3. Carrier-layer map
>
> ## Highest-value carrier layers
>
> **Packaging-as-campaign**
> This is one of the richest zones for your object class because text, object, and commercial function are naturally tied. Cadbury “Made to Share” and PENNY “Price Packs” are strong models: the pack is not just shown; it is the compositional idea. ([dandad.org][8])
>
> **OOH-lite / print / outdoor statics**
> Still the clearest carrier for integrated type-photo composition. IKEA’s price-tag work and Holland & Barrett’s body-part typography show how a static commercial frame can turn text into object or object into text. ([Creative Review][4])
>
> **Retail promo visuals and POS**
> High potential for mass and middle-market examples, especially grocery, pharmacy, beauty, home, and food. But indexing is weak unless the work wins awards or gets agency/trade coverage.
>
> **Paid social statics and carousels**
> Huge volume, especially 2024–2026, but high sludge. Use only with constraints: named brand, named campaign, known agency, or category plus date.
>
> **Production studio stills / commercial photography portfolios**
> Excellent for object-first aesthetics and mixed market levels. Weak for final typography unless the photographer or retoucher posts finished layouts.
>
> ---
>
> # 4. Source-class relevance, market tendency, and noise boundary
>
> | Source class                        | Why relevant                                  | Carrier coverage                                      | Market tendency                                   | Noise boundary                                      |
> | ----------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
> | Agency / brand case studies         | Best proof of real campaign logic and credits | Campaign statics, OOH, packaging, social, POS         | Mixed; strong middle/mass if searched by category | Case-film polish; missing variant depth             |
> | Award archives                      | Best filtered craft layer                     | Print, outdoor, packaging, typography, product design | Awardable mass + premium                          | Clever one-offs, student/spec, over-polished boards |
> | Production / still-life directories | Best product-object trail                     | Still-life, beauty, food, drink, tech, motion         | Luxury + everyday + middle                        | Image may lack final type                           |
> | Trade publications                  | Best recent discovery layer                   | OOH, campaign launches, brand platforms               | Middle/premium; some mass                         | Novelty bias, film-led articles                     |
> | Packaging/design publications       | Best object-bound type layer                  | Packs, labels, launch imagery, shelf systems          | FMCG, DTC, beauty, food                           | Mockups and identity-only cases                     |
> | Live ad libraries                   | Best live paid evidence                       | Social statics, video covers, carousels               | Mass/middle                                       | Banal overlay, offer spam, weak credits             |
> | Pinterest / visual boards           | Good for mood-fragment discovery              | Fragments of all of the above                         | Skews whatever is repinned                        | Bad source attribution; derivative fragments        |
>
> ---
>
> # 5. Explicit blind spots
>
> ## Poorly indexed zones
>
> **Retail promo statics**
> Supermarket, pharmacy, beauty retail, convenience, and QSR promo frames often disappear into email, in-store screens, local OOH, retailer apps, and paid-social variants. They rarely get archived unless they win awards or an agency posts them.
>
> **Middle-market e-commerce campaign assets**
> Not marketplace listing creative, but brand-owned campaign assets for DTC, beauty, home, food, accessories, and wellness. These often live briefly on homepages, social carousels, emails, and landing pages.
>
> **Regional OOH and transit campaigns**
> Many strong product/type frames are regional and never enter global design press. AdForum, Ads of the World, and award archives catch some, but not all.
>
> **Production/post-production portfolios**
> The people who made the image may publish the best stills, but not the final typographic campaign frame. This creates a split between **photographic source** and **designed commercial output**.
>
> **In-house agency work**
> Mass retailers and grocery brands increasingly make large volumes internally. Campaign In-House Awards’ 2025 M&S Food note is a useful signal: M&S’s in-house agency reportedly produces advertising, sponsorship, editorial, photography, CRM, and online content, which implies a lot of relevant product/type work may never be credited in traditional agency channels. ([Campaign Inhouse Agency Awards][9])
>
> ## Where Pinterest is likely derivative
>
> Pinterest is useful for visual drift, not provenance. It can surface fragments of product/type/photo work, but it often points to reposts, moodboards, third-party blogs, cropped images, or dead source chains. Pinterest itself positions the platform as visual discovery and visual search, which explains why it is good for finding adjacent aesthetics; but that same discovery behavior does not guarantee original campaign context. ([Pinterest][10])
>
> For this object class, Pinterest is most likely to show:
>
> * Cropped OOH frames without agency or brand context.
> * Packaging mockups detached from campaign use.
> * Designer portfolio fragments reposted without credits.
> * Old print ads misdated as contemporary references.
> * Luxury still-life fragments overrepresenting “tasteful” work.
>
> Use Pinterest as a **reverse-image-search trigger**, not as a source layer.
>
> ---
>
> # 6. Contradictions found
>
> **Contradiction 1: “Design inspiration” sites are visible but not necessarily operational.**
> They can show beautiful frames, but often fail on credits, carrier proof, and repeatable browsing. The better operational layers were award archives, trade publications, and production directories.
>
> **Contradiction 2: Live ad libraries are current but noisy.**
> They are the closest to real paid distribution, but they are bad for craft discovery unless constrained by brand/category/campaign. Meta, Google, and TikTok provide searchable ad/creative surfaces, but not a clean visual-art-direction archive. ([Facebook][7])
>
> **Contradiction 3: Still-life photography surfaces are visually strong but compositionally incomplete.**
> Production Paradise is excellent for object/product photography and commercial photographers, including luxury and everyday brands, but the final integrated typography may live elsewhere. ([Production Paradise][5])
>
> **Contradiction 4: Packaging work may be more relevant than posters.**
> For this brief, the pack/label/price/device often creates stronger text-photo unity than conventional print ads. PENNY and Cadbury are better proof than many “beautiful poster” examples because the product object and text system are materially inseparable. ([house-of-communication.com][1])
>
> ---
>
> # 7. Recommended next-pass plan for building a shortlist
>
> ## Pass 1: Build source buckets, not image boards
>
> Create separate buckets for:
>
> * **Packaging-as-campaign**
> * **OOH / print statics**
> * **Retail / POS / grocery / pharmacy**
> * **Beauty / wellness / cosmetics**
> * **Food / drink / FMCG**
> * **Home / furniture / objects**
> * **Production-led still-life systems**
> * **Paid social statics**
>
> Each candidate should be logged with: brand, campaign, agency, production/still-life credits, year, carrier, source URL, whether the type is materially integrated, and whether the product/object is central.
>
> ## Pass 2: Use award archives as filters
>
> Search D&AD, ADC/The One Club, ADCE, Epica, AdForum, Lürzer’s, and Ads of the World by:
>
> * Print & Outdoor
> * Typography / Lettering
> * Packaging
> * Product Design
> * Photography
> * Retail / FMCG / Beauty / Food / Home categories
> * 2024, 2025, 2026
>
> Do not collect “nice ad” entries unless the text and image are compositionally dependent.
>
> ## Pass 3: Cross-reference through production credits
>
> For every strong agency/award example, chase:
>
> * photographer
> * retoucher / CGI studio
> * production company
> * set designer
> * food stylist / prop stylist
> * design studio
> * motion/stills director
>
> This is likely to uncover more sibling work than searching “typography product campaign” broadly.
>
> ## Pass 4: Add live evidence only after brand targets exist
>
> Use Meta Ad Library, Google Ads Transparency Center, and TikTok Creative Center for brands already identified through the stronger layers. Search the brand, then manually filter for static/product/type frames. Do not use live ad libraries as the first discovery layer.
>
> ## Pass 5: Use Pinterest only as a provenance challenge
>
> When Pinterest surfaces a strong image, reverse-search it and require one of:
>
> * agency page
> * brand page
> * award archive
> * trade publication
> * production/photographer portfolio
> * credited Behance/case page from the actual studio
>
> No provenance, no shortlist.
>
> **Best next move:** build a 40–60 item “candidate atlas” across the source buckets above, then reduce it to a shortlist only after scoring each item on composition, carrier proof, market level, date, credits, and repeatable hunting value.

Я не стал механически дробить твой `field map` как есть. Сначала я применил runtime-исключения этой ветки, поэтому ниже уже **очищенные manual-web-search prompts для добычи ссылок**, без UI, marketplace, cinema drift, музейных архивов и generic ad-directory мусора.

**1. Agency / Brand Case Studies**
```text
Run a manual web-search pass to collect direct links to agency and brand case-study pages where product/object photography and typography are co-designed into one commercial visual system.

Target object:
Real commercial frames where text and product/object photo are compositionally inseparable. Carrier can vary: OOH, print, social statics, promo tiles, retail visuals, packaging-led campaign assets, launch pages.

Goal:
Build a kept link corpus of case-study pages that can serve as source-of-origin anchors for later reference hunting.

Priorities:
- 2024–2026, strongest bias to 2025–2026
- mixed market: luxury + middle-market + mass-commercial
- middle/mass is important; do not hide inside luxury-safe work
- prefer FMCG, beauty, wellness, food/drink, home, retail, consumer tech, accessories

Exclude:
- marketplace creatives
- web/UI galleries
- generic poster inspiration
- case films without usable static assets
- portfolio pages with no campaign context
- banal headline-over-photo work

What to return:
1. 20–30 kept links only.
2. For each link: brand, agency/studio, year, carrier, market level, and one-line proof of why text+photo are truly integrated.
3. Flag whether the page is a strong source-of-origin anchor or only a lead.
4. Prefer fewer stronger links over padding.

Anti-surface requirements:
- use source-constrained searches
- run one contradiction-seeking pass for middle/mass-commercial
- justify any obvious or high-visibility result that survives
```

**2. Trade / Editorial Campaign Coverage**
```text
Run a manual web-search pass to collect direct links to trade and editorial campaign coverage that shows real static commercial work where product/object photography and typography function as one composed frame.

Target object:
Recent campaign articles, launch writeups, and commercial coverage pages with visible static assets, credits, carrier notes, and enough context to trace the original work.

Goal:
Find publication surfaces that repeatedly expose this object class, especially outside the luxury-only layer.

Priorities:
- 2024–2026
- middle-market and mass-commercial must be actively included
- prefer retail, grocery, pharmacy, beauty, beverage, food, home, wellness, consumer goods
- strongest signal when the article includes static visuals + credits + carrier description

Exclude:
- design-inspiration blogs without campaign proof
- film-led campaign coverage where stills are secondary
- fashion/editorial-only imagery
- generic ad roundups
- text-over-image without compositional dependence

What to return:
1. 15–25 kept article links.
2. For each: publication, brand/campaign, year, carrier, whether it covers static visuals or only the idea, and whether it helps trace agency/production credits.
3. Separate:
   - strong repeatable publications
   - one-off useful articles
4. Note where novelty bias weakens the surface.

Anti-surface requirements:
- do not accept visible trade hits by default
- run source-constrained and deeper expansion passes
- prefer traceable campaign coverage over glossy commentary
```

**3. Production / Still-Life / Commercial Photography Credits Trail**
```text
Run a manual web-search pass to collect direct links to production, still-life, commercial photography, retouching, CGI, and post-production surfaces that can lead to real product+text campaign work.

Target object:
Commercial object/product imagery ecosystems that repeatedly feed beauty, food, drink, wellness, home, retail, accessories, and consumer-goods campaigns.

Goal:
Build a link corpus of photographers, production companies, reps, and post houses whose work can be cross-traced into finished commercial text+photo frames.

Important:
The page does not need to show final typography every time, but it must be operationally useful for finding sibling campaign work.

Priorities:
- 2024–2026
- mixed market levels, not luxury-only
- strong preference for client-linked work, campaign naming, and repeatable commercial categories

Exclude:
- abstract still-life with no commercial client context
- editorial/fashion portfolios without product-object focus
- art photography
- inspiration boards
- image-only pages with no traceable credits or client layer

What to return:
1. 15–25 kept links.
2. For each: photographer/studio/company, client/category, year, whether final type is visible or needs cross-tracing, and what next link-search path it opens.
3. Separate:
   - direct campaign-useful links
   - credit trails that need a second hop
4. Flag which links are best for middle/mass-commercial object work.

Anti-surface requirements:
- prefer operational value over pure beauty
- run contradiction-seeking searches against luxury drift
- justify any portfolio-style result that survives
```

**4. Packaging-As-Campaign / Object-Bound Typography**
```text
Run a manual web-search pass to collect direct links to commercial work where packaging, label systems, price devices, wrappers, cartons, sleeves, or other product-bound typography become the campaign composition itself.

Target object:
Not packaging design in isolation, but photographed or commercially deployed packaging-led visuals where object and type are materially inseparable.

Goal:
Find linkable source pages that show product/object + type unity in consumer-facing commercial use.

Priorities:
- 2024–2026
- FMCG, food/drink, beauty, wellness, home care, retail, pharmacy, consumer packaged goods
- middle-market and mass-commercial are essential, not optional

Exclude:
- packaging mockups with no live or campaign context
- identity-only case studies
- luxury bottle porn without carrier proof
- packaging trend galleries
- conceptual student work

What to return:
1. 15–25 kept links.
2. For each: brand, agency/studio, year, whether the pack/type system is shown in live photography or only as design presentation, and which carrier is visible.
3. Mark:
   - strong live/commercial proof
   - strong but still design-case-only
4. Prefer links that can later feed a shortlist of real commercial frames.

Anti-surface requirements:
- require proof that the packaging system entered a campaign, launch, retail, or promo context
- downgrade pretty mockups without deployment evidence
- use deeper expansion to find live usage if the first page is only a design case
```

**5. Live Deployment / Verification Pass**
```text
Run a constrained manual web-search pass to find live or near-live deployed examples of product/object + integrated typography, but only by using brands, campaigns, agencies, photographers, or production entities already discovered in earlier passes.

Target object:
Actual deployed statics and commercial frames: social ads, launch pages, brand campaign pages, archived landing pages, OOH reporting, retail promo visuals, or other live/public traces.

Goal:
Verify that strong candidates were not just case-study storytelling, but actually circulated as commercial visuals.

Rules:
- do not use this as open-ended discovery
- only search outward from already found entities
- marketplace remains excluded
- prioritize brand-owned, campaign-owned, archived, or transparency-style evidence

What to return:
1. Direct deployment links only.
2. For each: brand/campaign, year, carrier, whether the frame is still live, archived, reported, or ad-library-visible.
3. Mark whether the typography-photo integration survives in the deployed version or weakens outside the case study.
4. Keep the set small and high-confidence.

Anti-surface requirements:
- no open-ended browsing
- no moodboards or reposts
- if provenance is weak, drop the link
```

**Prompt notes**
- Это уже `Manual Web Search Prompt`-набор, не `Deep Research Prompt`.
- Порядок запуска: `1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5`.
- Если хочешь, следующим сообщением я соберу еще один слой: `master candidate-atlas prompt`, который будет не по одному bucket, а сразу под таблицу на 40–60 ссылок с колонками.

> ## Notes on the search logic
>
> The **source-constrained pass** favored agency and brand surfaces: VCCP, Ogilvy, Wieden+Kennedy, Grey, LePub, Serviceplan / House of Communication, Philips, and Unilever-owned brand pages. I also used award/trade pages only when they exposed a stronger source chain.
>
> The **middle/mass contradiction pass** was useful. It kept PENNY, Cadbury, Maynards Bassetts, Coca-Cola, Vaseline, Holland & Barrett, IKEA, Heinz, Co-op, Naturo, and KitKat in the corpus so the list did not collapse into luxury-safe still-life.
>
> The obvious survivors—**Cadbury, Coca-Cola, Heinz, IKEA, KitKat**—survived because the product/object is the commercial mechanism: wrapper-as-message, crushed logo-as-message, bottle/label-as-message, price tag-as-story, phone/object-as-break. They are not included merely because they are famous.
>
> I would treat the next pass as an **asset-verification pass**: open each anchor, save representative statics, then demote anything where the page only contains a case film, generic campaign copy, or unresolved headline-over-photo.

([shots][28]) | 2025 | AR, cinematic OOH, experiential, product QR packaging          | Keep as useful commercial product/collab carrier detail. Caveat: experiential/FOOH novelty may dominate over static craft.                            |

Caveat: film-led; AOTW *In My Bag* is a better static candidate.                 |
>
> ## Best repeatable surfaces from this pass
>
> **1. Ads of the World** — strongest repeatable index for your object class because it reliably tags **medium**, **industry**, **brand**, **agency**, and **media-asset count**. It is especially useful for middle-market and non-luxury campaigns: grocery, pharmacy, food, delivery, QSR, packaged goods. Caveat: the pages were blocked from direct fetch in this environment, so I would use the links as a manual review queue rather than treating the snippets as final proof.
>
> **2. LBB** — strongest when production craft matters. It often gives credits and behind-the-scenes context, and it repeatedly surfaces product photography/design-system campaigns. Caveat: it skews toward high-craft, premium beverage, film, and production-company stories.
>
> **3. Campaign / Campaign Live** — useful as a validation layer for UK retail/grocery OOH and print rollouts. It is good for carrier descriptions and campaign trade context. Caveat: asset depth is uneven and many pages are brief.
>
> **4. Creative Salon** — strong for UK commercial retail and supermarket work with full campaign/agency context. Caveat: articles can be more launch-commentary than asset-proof, so visual verification is needed.
>
> **5. Shots** — good for credits and production context, but weaker for this specific object class because it is often film/director-led. Keep only when stills, OOH, product photography, or packaging activations are explicitly named.
>
> ## Where novelty bias weakens the surface
>
> The biggest bias shows up around **FOOH, AR, special builds, celebrity films, and 360 launch language**. These articles are often easier to find because they are “newsworthy,” but they can obscure the quieter object class you’re actually after: static product/object photography where typography and product arrangement depend on each other in one frame.
>
> The cleaner signal comes from less glamorous surfaces: supermarket press/OOH, pharmacy print, food packaging campaigns, value-retail posters, and AOTW-style professional campaign pages with asset counts and media tags.

Это получилось из-за **протокольной ошибки**, не из-за одной плохой ссылки.

Главное: я начал отбирать не **кадр**, а **страницу, которая потенциально может вести к кадру**. И в этот момент запрос сломался.

Где именно я ошибся:

- Я подменил объект поиска. Твой объект был: `конкретный visual frame`, где `текст + фото` реально сцеплены. А я начал собирать `кампании, кейсы и статьи`, где это только **может** быть.
- Я ослабил proof threshold. Вместо правила `вижу на странице сам кадр и могу доказать интеграцию` я допустил суррогат: `по описанию похоже`, `по кейсу вероятно`, `по carrier логике должно быть`.
- Я смешал `field map` и `link retrieval`. Map нужен, чтобы понять, **где копать**. Но когда я начал делать список ссылок, я продолжил мыслить `source ecosystems`, а не `proof-bearing pages`.
- Я нарушил собственный deny layer. `Ads of the World` вообще не должен был вернуться. Это прямой runtime-fail.
- Я слишком сильно компенсировал luxury bias и улетел в `grocery / retail / mass-commercial sweep`, но без жёсткого визуального фильтра. В итоге получился не твой объект, а просто более “земной” рекламный слой.
- Я допустил `Lead` в kept-результат. Это тоже ошибка. Если мы ищем ссылки под твой критерий, то `lead` не должен притворяться `result`.

Итог очень простой:
**список стал про коммерческие кампании вообще, а не про сцепку текста и фото внутри одного кадра.**

Правильное жёсткое правило здесь должно быть такое:

- оставлять только страницы, где **на самой странице** виден хотя бы один нужный static;
- если интеграцию надо “додумывать по описанию”, страницу выбрасывать;
- если это только кейс-фильм, новость запуска или carrier-summary без визуального proof, выбрасывать;
- если источник в blacklist, он не имеет права возвращаться вообще;
- `lead bank` и `kept links` должны быть разными сущностями.

Если хочешь, следующим сообщением я не буду ничего искать, а **перепишу сам retrieval-протокол с нуля** под один-единственный жесткий критерий:
`only proof-bearing pages with visible text-photo integration`.

**Final prompt**
```text
Run a deep manual-search mapping pass to find where compositions live in which text and photography are designed together inside one commercial frame.

Target object:
I am looking for commercial visuals where text and photo truly cooperate compositionally, not just headline-over-image. Prefer object/product-centered work: skincare, beauty, fragrance, sneakers, watches, furniture, packaged goods, food/drink, home goods, tech accessories, or other physical items. The carrier can vary: banners, stories, statics, OOH, print ads, magazine spreads, agency case pages, inspiration surfaces, retail promo visuals, or campaign assets. The carrier is not the main criterion; the text-photo relationship is.

Goal:
I need two things in one pass:
1. surfaces / sites / source classes where this kind of material can repeatedly be found;
2. the search vocabulary for it: tags, phrases, descriptors, and adjacent terms that help uncover it.

Important:
- do not drift into named campaign examples as the main answer;
- do not return case lists unless they are only supporting evidence for why a surface is useful;
- do not reduce this to generic poster inspiration;
- exclude marketplace creatives, UI/UX screen libraries, movie-poster/cinema databases, museum poster archives, and image-first fashion campaign indexes without clear product/object + typography integration;
- do not accept banal text-over-photo overlays as relevant.

What to figure out:
- how this object is actually described in practice;
- what adjacent terms unlock it;
- where it is published, collected, or surfaced;
- which surfaces are useful for repeated hunting rather than one-off inspiration.

What to return:
1. A kept list of the strongest surfaces / sites / source classes for finding this material.
2. For each one: what kind of object-led text+photo work appears there, what market layer it covers (luxury / middle / mass), and why it is operationally useful.
3. A query-vocabulary bank grouped by intent:
   - direct descriptors
   - adjacent/industry phrases
   - commercial/carrier phrases
   - product-photography phrases
   - negative terms to exclude junk
4. A short naming section:
   - what this visual object is most likely called in English search language
   - which labels are too broad or misleading
5. If useful, separate:
   - best surfaces for proof-bearing examples
   - best surfaces for broader hunting
   - best query families for manual searching

Anti-surface requirements:
- Do not treat visible or top-ranked results as sufficient by default.
- Run source-constrained, contradiction-seeking, and deeper expansion passes.
- Prefer fewer stronger surfaces and cleaner vocabulary over padded completeness.
```

**Prompt notes**
- Mode: `Manual Web Search Prompt`
- Output object: `sites/surfaces + query vocabulary`, not cases
- Freshness: bias to `2024–2026`, especially `2025–2026`
- Exclusion bias: marketplace, UI/UX, cinema, museum-poster, generic text-over-image

> вот ответ
> The cleanest English search-language for your target is not one fixed category. It is usually found at the intersection of **product key visual**, **advertising still life**, **campaign art direction**, **brand photography**, **packaging / brand system**, and **OOH / print / static images**. The strongest sources are the ones that let you filter or infer **medium + industry + credits + still assets**, not just moodboard images.
>
> ## Kept surfaces / source classes
>
> | Surface / source class                                             | What appears there                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |                                 Market layer | Why it is operationally useful                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
> | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------: | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
> | **Ads of the World**                                               | Campaign pages with media tags such as **Print**, **Static Images**, **OOH Outdoor**, industry filters, agency names, and asset counts. It is especially useful for food, beauty, pharmacy, household, retail, packaged goods, and non-luxury ads. |                 Mass / middle / some premium | Best repeatable proof surface when the question is: “Was this a real campaign asset?” AOTW’s campaign search exposes medium and industry structure, and current search pages show filters for Print, Static Images, OOH Outdoor, Beauty, Food, Health, Household, etc. ([Ads of the World™][1])                                                                                                                 |
> | **Communication Arts — Exhibits / Projects**                       | Awarded commercial work with captions, art direction notes, production notes, and credits. Good for print, OOH, packaging, identity, and campaign visuals where composition is discussed.                                                          |           Middle / premium / agency-led mass | Strong when you need more than a pretty image. For example, CA’s Flamingo OOH page discusses commercial product photography experience and visual influences, which is exactly the kind of production-context signal that helps separate composed product work from generic overlays. ([Communication Arts][2])                                                                                                 |
> | **Fonts In Use**                                                   | Real-world typography in advertising, packaging, identity, object/product, retail, print, and digital contexts. Often includes source links, typefaces, designers, agencies, and sometimes photography credits.                                    | All layers, with strong design-literate bias | Best for searching from the **type side** rather than the campaign side. The site explicitly catalogs typography across “branding, advertising, signage, packaging, publications, in print and online,” and its taxonomy includes Product, Retail/Shopping, Advertising, Object/Product, Packaging, Posters/Flyers, and Signs. ([fontsinuse.com][3])                                                            |
> | **BP&O**                                                           | Long-form identity and packaging criticism with embedded project imagery, art direction notes, product-photography commentary, agency attribution, and brand-system context.                                                                       | Premium / middle / design-led consumer goods | Good for finding **designed systems** where typography, packaging, photography, and art direction are discussed together. BP&O’s Sigma article, for example, covers visual identity, packaging, custom typography, product launch campaigns, and how the system works across product and spatial contexts. ([Richard Baird][4])                                                                                 |
> | **The Brand Identity**                                             | Brand/campaign case studies and interviews with heavy visual galleries. Strong for product-led identity, packaging, photography direction, type systems, and art-directed launch worlds.                                                           |          Middle / premium / contemporary DTC | Useful as a hunting surface for “brand world” cases, especially skincare, food/drink, wellness, tech accessories, and boutique CPG. It is less proof-bearing than trade press but stronger for seeing full visual systems.                                                                                                                                                                                      |
> | **World Brand Design Society**                                     | Packaging, product-photography, food-styling, brand-system, and retail-facing case pages. Often includes deliverables, format, industry, region, keywords, and credits.                                                                            |              Middle / mass / emerging brands | Useful because its metadata maps directly to your object class: “Campaign,” “Digital,” “Packaging,” “Photography,” “Product,” “Typography,” “Food Styling,” and “Product Photography” recur as project deliverables/filters. Example pages describe shelf-ready supermarket systems with bold typography and product/ingredient cues. ([World Brand Design Society][5])                                         |
> | **The Dieline**                                                    | Packaging and CPG identity coverage across food, beverage, beauty, health, home, and private label. Sometimes includes redesign/campaign context and agency/studio attribution.                                                                    |                  Mass / middle / premium CPG | Best for **packaging-as-frame** and retail-facing product systems. It is less pure campaign proof than AOTW, but very strong for mass and middle-market categories. Dieline surfaces Walmart private label, food, beauty/health, beverage, and packaging-agency directory entries that explicitly include product photography, typography, branding, packaging, and retail/environmental design. ([DIELINE][6]) |
> | **Behance, but only with strict filters**                          | Agency/student/freelance case decks, product key visuals, OOH mockups, campaign statics, CGI product visuals, cosmetics launch visuals, social statics, and branded still-life systems.                                                            |         Mass / speculative / middle / global | High volume, low proof. Use only when filtered by terms such as **product key visual**, **advertising key visual**, **campaign art direction**, **product photography**, **OOH campaign**, and then verify elsewhere. Behance search pages show 10,000+ results for “product key visual,” with tags including cosmetics, advertising, photography, ads design, and beauty. ([Behance][7])                       |
> | **Agency / design-studio case pages**                              | Original case pages showing the system: campaign images, packaging, art direction, typography, grid, photography, launch assets, OOH, in-store, social statics.                                                                                    |   Depends on agency; often middle to premium | Most useful for tracing original intent and credits. Pentagram pages, for example, often list client, sector, discipline, partner, project team, and explain how typography, photography, packaging, and campaign assets work together. ([Pentagram][8])                                                                                                                                                        |
> | **Photographer / production-company portfolios**                   | “Advertising still life,” “print advertising,” “key visual photography,” beauty/product print campaigns, set design, retouching, and production notes.                                                                                             |     Premium / middle; some mass via agencies | Best when you are hunting the **photographic composition layer** rather than publication coverage. Photographer interviews and production pages describe how campaign concepts come from agencies, then photographers contribute treatments, image compositions, stylists, and set design. ([wexphotovideo.com][9])                                                                                             |
> | **Brand-photography / visual-identity essays and guideline pages** | Language around brand photography as part of identity systems: key visuals, product-focused imagery, tone, typography, visual language, campaign consistency.                                                                                      |                Mostly design-led / strategic | Useful for vocabulary extraction. Werklig’s brand-photography essay explicitly places brand images alongside logo, typography, and tone of voice, and distinguishes product-focused brands with high-level imagery and key visuals from lifestyle brands. ([werklig.com][10])                                                                                                                                   |
> | **Retail / visual-merchandising publications**                     | Window campaigns, in-store graphics, product displays, billboard-style campaign imagery, product + type in physical environments.                                                                                                                  |               Mass / middle / premium retail | Useful for carriers where the composed frame becomes a window, wall, table, shelf, or display. Weaker for static asset downloads, but strong for product-object + type in commercial retail space. Retail Design Blog examples discuss window campaigns, campaign imagery walls, merchandise displays, and logotype/display integration. ([retaildesignblog.net][11])                                           |
>
> ## Best surfaces for proof-bearing examples
>
> Use these when you need evidence that the visual was a real campaign/commercial asset:
>
> 1. **Ads of the World** — best repeatable campaign index for medium, industry, agency, and asset count.
> 2. **Communication Arts** — best for edited/awarded work with production context and credits.
> 3. **Agency or studio case pages** — best for original intent, system logic, and project team.
> 4. **LBB / Campaign / Creative Salon / Shots** — useful for trade validation, but watch for film-led novelty bias.
> 5. **Photographer / production-company portfolios** — best for still-life craft, set design, retouching, and “key visual” language.
>
> ## Best surfaces for broader hunting
>
> Use these when you are building a large visual map rather than verifying one campaign:
>
> 6. **Fonts In Use** — search from typography outward.
> 7. **BP&O / The Brand Identity / World Brand Design Society** — search from identity and packaging outward.
> 8. **The Dieline** — search from CPG, shelf, packaging, and retail outward.
> 9. **Behance** — use only after narrowing vocabulary; it is high-volume but polluted by mockups, speculative work, and banal overlays.
> 10. **Retail visual-merchandising sites** — useful for spatial carriers and store-window campaign graphics.
>
> ---
>
> # Query vocabulary bank
>
> ## 1. Direct descriptors
>
> These are the closest search terms for the object itself:
>
> * **product key visual**
> * **advertising key visual**
> * **campaign key visual**
> * **product campaign key visual**
> * **commercial still life**
> * **advertising still life**
> * **still life advertising**
> * **product still life campaign**
> * **art directed product photography**

> * **product photography + typography**
> * **brand photography key visuals**
> * **object-led campaign**

> * **packaging and campaign art direction**
> * **hero product image**
> * **hero product visual**
> * **brand world photography**

>

> * `"brand photography" "key visuals" "typography"`
> * `"product-led" "visual identity" "photography"`

> Best combinations:
>
> * `"advertising still life" "set design"`
> * `"beauty still life" "typography"`
> * `"fragrance still life" "campaign"`
> * `"tabletop photography" "campaign" "typography"`
> * `"packshot" "key visual"`
> * `"product marketing photography" "static images"`
>
> ## 5. Negative terms to exclude junk
>
> Use these when search results drift into the wrong world:
>
> * `-movie`
> * `-film`
> * `-cinema`
> * `-poster archive`
> * `-museum`
> * `-marketplace`
> * `-etsy`
> * `-template`
> * `-mockup`
> * `-canva`
> * `-ui`
> * `-ux`
> * `-app`
> * `-screen`
> * `-website template`
> * `-landing page`
> * `-stock`
> * `-freepik`
> * `-shutterstock`
> * `-pinterest`
> * `-wallpaper`
> * `-fashion editorial`
> * `-runway`
> * `-lookbook`
> * `-"text overlay"`
> * `-"social media template"`
> * `-"poster inspiration"`
>
> A practical query pattern:
>
> **`"product key visual" "typography" -template -mockup -movie -ui -pinterest`**
>
> ---
>
> # Naming: what this object is most likely called
>
> The most useful English names are:
>
> 1. **Product key visual** — best for campaign/launch/commercial use. It implies a central product image designed to travel across carriers.
> 2. **Advertising still life** — best when the product/object photograph is staged and composed as the main frame.
> 3. **Commercial still life** — broader than advertising still life; useful for photographer and production searches.
> 4. **Product photography art direction** — best when searching for case studies or production notes.
> 5. **Brand photography / brand imagery system** — best when the work is part of a larger identity system rather than a single ad.
> 6. **Campaign art direction** — best for agency/studio case pages, but must be paired with product terms to avoid film/talent work.
> 7. **Packaging + campaign visual system** — useful when typography and product photography are integrated through pack, shelf, poster, and social assets.
>
> ## Labels that are too broad or misleading
>
> * **Poster design** — too broad; pulls cultural posters, student posters, museum archives, and film posters.
> * **Graphic design inspiration** — too broad and weak on commercial proof.
> * **Typography poster** — usually type-only or cultural, not product-object commercial.
> * **Product photography** — too broad; pulls ecommerce packshots and marketplace images.
> * **Still life photography** — too broad; pulls editorial, art, fashion, and portfolio work.
> * **Branding** — too broad unless paired with product photography, campaign, packaging, or key visual.
> * **Creative ads** — too broad; tends to return award-bait and concept-only ads.
> * **Social media design** — often template-heavy and overlay-heavy.
> * **Text overlay** — almost the opposite of your target; it usually signals non-integrated headline-over-image.
>
> ---
>
> # Query families for manual searching
>
> ## Proof-first campaign search
>
> Use when you want real, traceable commercial examples:
>
> * `site:adsoftheworld.com/campaigns "Static Images" "Product"`
> * `site:adsoftheworld.com/campaigns "Print" "Beauty"`
> * `site:adsoftheworld.com/campaigns "OOH Outdoor" "Food"`
> * `site:campaignlive.co.uk "product photography" "OOH"`
> * `site:lbbonline.com "product photography" "print campaign"`
> * `site:commarts.com "product photography" "advertising"`
>
> ## Design-system search
>
> Use when you want the frame logic: type, product, photography, packaging, system.
>
> * `site:bpando.org "product photography" "typography"`
> * `site:the-brandidentity.com "product photography" "typography"`
> * `site:worldbranddesign.com "product photography" "typography"`
> * `site:thedieline.com "product photography" "typography"`
> * `site:fontsinuse.com/uses "packaging" "product photography"`
>
> ## Product-key-visual search
>
> Use when looking for composed commercial hero frames:
>
> * `"product key visual" "typography"`
> * `"advertising key visual" "product photography"`
> * `"campaign key visual" "beauty"`
> * `"product KV" "typography"`
> * `"key visual photography" "product"`
> * `"hero product visual" "campaign"`
>
> ## Still-life production search
>
> Use when looking for photographers, set design, and production craft:
>
> * `"advertising still life" "typography"`
> * `"commercial still life" "campaign"`
> * `"beauty still life" "art direction"`
> * `"fragrance still life" "set design"`
> * `"tabletop still life" "advertising"`
> * `"packshot art direction" "campaign"`
>
> ## Retail / mass-market search
>
> Use when you want to escape luxury-only surfaces:
>
> * `"private label redesign" "product photography" "typography"`
> * `"FMCG branding" "product photography" "typography"`
> * `"supermarket campaign" "print" "product photography"`
> * `"grocery campaign" "OOH" "static"`
> * `"shopper marketing" "product photography" "typography"`
> * `"retail promo visuals" "product photography"`
> * `"in-store campaign" "product photography" "typography"`
>
> ## Bottom line
>
> For repeated hunting, I would use this stack:
>
> **Proof:** Ads of the World → Communication Arts → agency/studio case pages.
> **Systems:** BP&O → The Brand Identity → World Brand Design Society → The Dieline.
> **Typography-led discovery:** Fonts In Use.
> **Volume discovery:** Behance, but only with “product key visual,” “advertising key visual,” “commercial still life,” and negative filters.
> **Production craft:** photographer / retoucher / set-design portfolios using “advertising still life,” “key visual photography,” and “product photography art direction.”

Ты ищешь не просто `product key visual` и не просто `advertising still life`.
Ты ищешь **poster-like commercial statics**, где:

- фото и типографика собраны как **один плакатный кадр**;
- текст не наложен сверху, а работает как часть композиционной архитектуры;
- часто есть `oversized type`, `type behind object`, `type wrapping the object`, `type as backdrop`, `type interacting with crop/perspective/negative space`;
- желательно есть **конкретный предмет / товар**, но допустимы и соседние форматы вроде cover-like promo statics, если композиционная логика та же.

Ниже уже **исправленный prompt**, сдвинутый именно в эту сторону.

**Final prompt**
```text
Conduct a deep research study to identify where poster-like commercial statics can be found in which typography and photography are co-authored as one composition.

Target object:
I am not looking for generic “text over image,” generic product photography, generic branding, or campaign case studies in general. I am looking for static commercial visuals that behave like promotional posters: the photo and the type are compositionally interdependent. The type may sit behind the object, wrap around it, scale across the frame, act as a backdrop, interact with crop/perspective/negative space, or otherwise function as part of the image architecture.

Preferred object class:
Physical product / object is strongly preferred: skincare, beauty, fragrance, drinks, food, sneakers, watches, furniture, home objects, tech devices, packaging-led promos, retail promo statics. Adjacent formats are allowed only if they clearly share the same poster-like composition logic.

Goal:
Return the best source surfaces and the best search vocabulary for finding this exact visual object.

Do not return:
- generic case-study lists
- generic ad campaigns
- UI/UX galleries
- marketplace creatives
- movie-poster / cinema databases
- museum poster archives
- fashion-editorial image banks without clear object/type integration
- broad Behance/Pinterest-style sludge
- generic packaging or branding sites unless they repeatedly show this exact composition type

What to return:
1. The strongest sites / surfaces / source classes where this material repeatedly appears.
2. For each source: what kind of poster-like text+photo work appears there, whether it is object-led, and why it is useful for repeated hunting.
3. A query vocabulary bank, grouped into:
   - core terms
   - adjacent useful terms
   - multilingual or regional terms if they materially improve recall
   - negative terms to exclude junk
4. A naming section:
   - what this object is most likely called in real search language
   - which labels are too broad and should be avoided
5. Separate:
   - primary hunt surfaces
   - adjacent support surfaces
   - surfaces to avoid by default

Requirements:
- prioritize 2024–2026, especially 2025–2026
- include Asian commercial poster ecosystems if they are relevant
- prefer fewer strong, operational surfaces over padded completeness
- justify why a surface is truly aligned with this composition type rather than merely nearby
```

**Prompt notes**
- Mode: `Deep Research Prompt`
- True object: `poster-like commercial statics`, not generic campaigns
- Output object: `sites/surfaces + search vocabulary`
- Strong visual bias: `object-led type-photo composition`
